fields.question: Why do process supervision methods label steps rather than only outcomes?
fields.answer: Failure doesn't identify the broken step. Local labels provide finer learning and selection, requiring annotations or reliable process judges. Do not broadcast terminal correctness as step truth.
fields.example: If step three fails, steps one and two needn't be marked wrong.

fields.question: What tradeoff separates active uncertain-step labeling from random labeling?
fields.answer: Active selection spends budget on hard judgments; random selection better reflects the original distribution. Uncertainty isn't importance and selection bias/label quality remain.
fields.example: An ambiguous formatting step can be less valuable to review than a key mathematical transition.

fields.question: How separate PRM labels and predictions?
fields.answer: Step truth is fixed supervision, probabilities differentiable, and entropy used only in allowed acquisition. Test step labels cannot select training samples. Candidate budget tests mechanism only.
fields.example: Training on observed test-label errors leaks evaluation.

fields.question: Why actively label uncertain steps instead of only checking final answers?
fields.answer: Final outcomes don't locate early mistakes. Step labels provide detailed reward-model supervision; uncertainty targets current ambiguous decisions but isn't a universal error proxy. Control candidate/evaluation budgets; no full local annotation dataset.
fields.example: Review an uncertain key algebraic move rather than repeatedly labeling obvious format.

fields.question: Why does OPST generate both problems and privileged clues?
fields.answer: Reduce reliance on human problem banks and give teacher extra solving context while students generate from prompts only. Validate generated tasks through independent re-answering, meaning-preserving rewrites and difficulty filtering.
fields.example: Resolve a generated problem independently to reject inconsistent prompts or answers.

fields.question: How does OPST easy filtering differ from removing student consensus?
fields.answer: Only unanimous matches to the candidate answer are too easy. Unanimous disagreement may signal a gap or bad problem. Removing all consensus changes the gate.
fields.example: Identical wrong results don't establish mastery.

fields.question: Is OPST EMA β old-teacher momentum or new-student weight?
fields.answer: It is new-student weight: after each student update, use (1−β) old teacher + β new student. Normalize per response then average equally. Document formula ambiguity instead of claiming unquestioned exactness.
fields.example: Small β means slowly absorb the student, not almost replace the teacher.

fields.question: Why reject as easy only unanimous matches to the verified candidate answer?
fields.answer: Agreement alone doesn't show mastery. All students can agree on the wrong answer. Privileged clues only guide teacher scoring on student prefixes; self-generated problems need independent re-answering and meaning-preserving checks.
fields.example: A unanimous wrong number remains useful until compared with the verified candidate answer.

fields.question: Why does UserArena report more than next-action accuracy?
fields.answer: Simulation should preserve trajectory dynamics, cross-session preferences and cohort differences, and reproduce differences between recommendation policies. Local hits aren't whole-user fidelity.
fields.example: Good click prediction with wrong long-run interest drift can still distort policy evaluation.

fields.question: How does OPTD teacher intent differ from giving the student future trajectories?
fields.answer: Only frozen teacher sees abstract intent, excluding concrete action/item identity, price and outcome. Student continues its own prefixes. Trust regions bound effects but don't prove no extraction leakage.
fields.example: Lightweight-item preference is allowed, next clicked product is not.

fields.question: May OPTD grounding replace gold tokens on a student rollout prefix?
fields.answer: No. Grounding uses separate true-prefix logits; teacher views score identical student prefixes. Use feasible lower endpoint per token with KL from mixed to no-intent teacher, not batch-mean reverse KL.
fields.example: Injecting the actual next action after a divergent student history is not teacher forcing on a real trajectory.

fields.question: Why give only teacher abstract intent and bound it token by token?
fields.answer: Whole trajectories leak future products/actions. Filter abstract preferences for teacher only, preserving student deployment input. Compare teacher views on the same prefix, constrain added guidance and ground on actual responses. KL can't replace leakage checks.
fields.example: Durability preference may be available; next item IDs and purchase outcomes may not.

fields.question: Why inspect RL and distillation gradient geometry in GIFT?
fields.answer: Teacher signal can conflict or add an orthogonal direction. Select by local logit gradients to reduce conflict and narrow supervision rather than imitate every token.
fields.example: Teacher format preferences can oppose task reward, so inspect the directions.

fields.question: How does GIFT token selection differ from projecting teacher gradients?
fields.answer: Selected tokens retain original distillation losses; gradients aren't rotated. Exact quotas may admit weak conflicts, so there is no universal finite-step safety guarantee.
fields.example: An accepted position uses its original loss, not a geometrically replaced gradient.

fields.question: Can GIFT renormalize by selected token count?
fields.answer: No. Divide by all valid tokens. Quotas depend on subbatch valid/eligible sets. Follow explicit handling for missing RL and zero teacher gradients rather than automatically treating them as novel directions.
fields.example: Selecting half and dividing by half doubles retained contribution.

fields.question: Why can't gradient-based GIFT selection promise permanent absence of conflict?
fields.answer: Prioritize nonconflicting and orthogonally informative tokens; quotas can require weaker conflicts. Selection isn't projection, and normalize by all valid tokens. Local logit geometry doesn't guarantee finite shared-parameter updates.
fields.example: A subbatch quota larger than conflict-free availability can select the least conflicting extras.

fields.question: Why minimally repair a wrong student response before projected distillation?
fields.answer: Expert prose can be far from student distribution. Minimal edits retain current behavior while correcting what is needed, with independent verification. This is an approximation, not exact most-likely correct output.
fields.example: Correct one wrong symbol instead of replacing the whole derivation.

fields.question: How does edited-span DPO differ from SFT on a complete repaired answer?
fields.answer: Span DPO contrasts only original and verified edit positions; unchanged text is not directly included. Full SFT is for student-generated successes, not projector repairs.
fields.example: An externally repaired reply is not an autonomous success from this round.

fields.question: Can edited-span scoring drop the preceding text?
fields.answer: No. Score each edit under its own complete causal prefix, summing span logp without length averaging. One insertion/deletion side may be empty but pair needs an edit. Zero direct gradient elsewhere does not protect shared weights.
fields.example: Editing step three changes step four's context; don't borrow another response's prefix.

fields.question: Why restrict DPO to edits and SFT to student successes?
fields.answer: Minimal repair preserves generated structure and focuses preference credit on corrections. Repaired and independently correct responses have different provenance. Score both sides under their full causal contexts; shared parameters can still change.
fields.example: If only the last operator is wrong, verify its replacement and contrast the edit rather than imitate all teacher wording.

fields.question: Why doesn't inter-layer OPTD only align final predictions?
fields.answer: Final agreement can hide different depth-wise revisions. Supervise shallow-to-deep log-probability increments and retain final OPD. This is prediction paths, not hidden-vector matching.
fields.example: Two models can end on A after very different intermediate changes.

fields.question: How does transition supervision differ from independent top-k at each layer?
fields.answer: Final student layer chooses fixed token identities for the entire path. Independent sets mix different objects when comparing increments.
fields.example: If shallow top is A and deep top B, subtracting their logp doesn't measure A's change.

fields.question: Which OPTD increment endpoints receive gradients and how is practical scale handled?
fields.answer: Both adjacent student readouts are differentiable. Teacher, candidate weights and correction coefficients are frozen. Appendix sums transitions while main text averages; neither is exact reverse transition KL.
fields.example: A sum of three transitions cannot silently become a mean at the same objective scale.

fields.question: Why choose candidate tokens once at the final student layer?
fields.answer: Track the same predictions through depth. Independent top-k confounds identity with changes. Use full-vocabulary-normalized log-probability increments plus final OPD, with detach and destination-layer weights, not hidden MSE or exact transition KL.
fields.example: If shallow favors A and deep B, retain both identities to trace their rise/fall.
